Efficient Dynamic Algorithms for Graph Neural Networks with Non-Linear Propagation

Kiarash Banihashem ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park Email: kiarash@umd.edu    MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park Email: hajiagha@umd.edu    Mahdi JafariRaviz11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park Email: mahdij@umd.edu    Silvio Lattanzi11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Google Research Email: silviol@google.com    Danny Mittal11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park Email: mittal@umd.edu
Abstract

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used for representation learning on graphs, but most methods assume static topologies, making them inefficient on evolving networks where edges change over time. Existing dynamic approaches either model graph evolution through temporal GNN architectures without focusing on efficient dynamic maintenance, or are restricted to linear propagation models based on Personalized PageRank.

In this work, we study how to efficiently maintain node representations for non-linear GNN propagation under edge insertions and deletions. The propagation has no learned parameters, and only a classifier applied afterward is trained. For a broad class of standard activation functions, we develop a residual-based dynamic algorithm that selectively propagates local errors via push operations, maintaining an approximation to the evolving fixed point without full recomputation. We prove that our method achieves amortized O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\epsilon) update time per graph change under a degree-normalized error guarantee. Our approach uses a potential-based analysis in a degree-scaled norm and, in contrast to prior work on the linear case, requires no randomness assumptions on either the update sequence or the input vector. For the linear special case, we additionally provide an exact dynamic algorithm via low-rank matrix inverse updates. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that incorporating non-linearity improves accuracy while preserving efficient update performance, yielding a scalable and theoretically grounded method for maintaining this propagation on dynamic graphs.

1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used in machine learning, both for prediction tasks such as node classification and as general-purpose tools for representation learning [12, 15]. Their ability to exploit the underlying graph structure of real-world data makes them effective in many domains such as biology, social sciences, and transportation [31]. A key challenge, however, is that real-world data is often dynamic: the relationships between the nodes of the graph are constantly changing, requiring the model to update its outputs accordingly. A naive way of satisfying this requirement is to periodically recompute the model after each change in order to incorporate changes in the graph. However, such recomputation is computationally expensive and therefore undesirable both theoretically and practically.

Existing approaches to dynamic GNNs can be broadly divided into two lines of work. The first line is temporal GNNs which model graph evolution using recurrent architectures, attention mechanisms, or memory modules [16, 27, 9, 21]. These approaches are primarily geared toward prediction tasks such as node classification and are not designed for efficiently maintaining representations under graph changes [34, 35]. The second line focuses on the propagation component of GNNs and considers linear GNNs where each node has a value obtained via iterated neighborhood averaging [34, 35]. In this setting, the model reduces to Personalized PageRank (PPR), where the structure enables efficient updates, allowing the representation vectors to be maintained under graph changes without recomputing from scratch [3, 33].

A natural question is whether one can efficiently maintain the representations of non-linear GNNs under graph updates. Non-linearity is central to the success of GNNs, as it enables the model to capture complex patterns in the data. By repeatedly composing non-linear activations with neighborhood aggregation, GNNs gain expressive power analogous to deep neural networks in standard (non-graph) settings.

Our Contributions.

In this paper, we answer the above question affirmatively. We study GNNs in which each node applies a non-linear activation to a weighted average of its neighbors. The propagation has no learned parameters, and its fixed point is unique. Training happens only in a classifier applied to the propagated features, as in InstantGNN [34]. We assume the activation function is KK-Lipschitz for some K≤1K\leq 1, a condition that is sufficient for convergence. This restriction is mild in the GNN setting. Common activations such as ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, hard tanh, softplus, softsign, and ELU are 1-Lipschitz or smaller. Under this assumption, we show that one can maintain an approximate solution for all nodes in amortized time O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\epsilon), where ϵ\epsilon is the degree-normalized approximation parameter. More precisely, the amortized time is O⁡((1+Bz)/(1−K⁡(1−α))2⋅(1/ϵ))O\big((1+B_{z})/(1-K(1-\alpha))^{2}\cdot(1/\epsilon)\big), where α\alpha is the teleportation probability and BzB_{z} bounds the size of the fixed point (Section 2.1). For K=1K=1, as for ReLU and tanh, the factor 1−K⁡(1−α)1-K(1-\alpha) equals α\alpha. In addition, for the linear special case, we provide an exact dynamic maintenance algorithm based on low-rank matrix-inverse updates, obtaining a worst-case update time O⁡(n1.5275)O(n^{1.5275}), where nn is the number of nodes. We complement our theoretical results with empirical evidence demonstrating the importance of non-linearity for achieving high accuracy. On large dynamic graph benchmarks, we show the practical behavior of our proposed approximation algorithm.

Our Techniques.

To maintain an approximate solution under dynamic updates, we use a residual vector, as in prior work [34, 33]. We use a push operation to propagate large residuals, and we show that when all residuals are small relative to the degree-scaled error, the maintained solution is a valid approximation. For an edge update, two effects must be handled: (i) the new values that should be propagated through the updated edge, and (ii) the effect of the degree changes at the two endpoints on their neighbors, which arises from the edge-weight normalization. The first effect can be handled in O⁡(1)O(1) time using the scaling trick of [33], which is not part of the main algorithm of [34]. After applying the effect of the edge update, the residuals at the endpoints may increase, and we propagate them when needed. The main difference from prior work is in the analysis of this cleanup step. Our setting requires handling the nonlinear update rule, and we also remove the randomness assumption used in prior work. We remove this assumption and obtain a deterministic guarantee, at the cost of a weaker amortized update bound.

Related Work

A line of work in dynamic GNNs studies temporal graphs, where the primary focus is on prediction tasks over evolving graphs [16, 27, 9, 21]. These approaches are typically divided into discrete-time dynamic (DTD) and continuous-time dynamic (CTD) models: the former takes as input a sequence of graph snapshots at different time steps, while the latter operates on a stream of timestamped events that modify the graph. We refer to [36] for a comprehensive overview. These models use the timing and order of graph changes as a signal for prediction, and some of them, such as [21], keep a memory for each node that depends on past events. In contrast to this line of work, our focus is not on prediction accuracy but on efficiently maintaining node embeddings under graph updates with theoretical guarantees. In particular, we provide amortized update time guarantees for our algorithm. The embeddings we maintain depend only on the current graph, so our method fits tasks where the history of changes does not matter, while temporal GNNs fit tasks where it does.

The closest line of work to ours is the literature on dynamic Personalized PageRank (PPR), which can be viewed as a special case of our model with update function fi​(x)=xf_{i}(x)=x. For this problem, [33] build on the Push framework of [2] and give a dynamic algorithm that maintains the PageRank solution for a randomly chosen source node. In our notation, this corresponds to setting ss to a random basis vector. Their algorithm has amortized update time O⁡(1/(n​ϵ))O(1/(n\epsilon)) when β∈{0,1}\beta\in\{0,1\}, where β\beta is the normalization parameter in Equation 1. Building on this line of work, [34] study a linear GNN model and obtain the same O⁡(1/(n​ϵ))O(1/(n\epsilon)) update time for general β\beta, but under an additional randomness assumption on the edge updates: each edge is assumed to be equally likely to be inserted at each time. In contrast to these works, we allow nonlinear updates and make no randomness assumptions on either the update sequence or the vector ss.

A separate line of work on dynamic PageRank uses random walk sampling to maintain the solution vector [3, 4, 14]. On a high level, this approach estimates each node’s solution value by averaging over a collection of random walks starting from the node. When an edge is inserted or deleted, only the affected walks are re-sampled in order to maintain correctness. This line of work was initiated by [3], who analyzed the setting under random edge updates. More recently, [14] extend this approach to general (adversarial) updates and obtain upper and lower bounds for both additive ℓ1\ell_{1} error and multiplicative error. The sampling technique heavily relies on the linearity of PageRank, which allows a node’s solution to be computed independently of its neighbors’ solutions. As such, this approach does not extend to the nonlinear setting considered in our work.

Relation to other GNN models.

As in the GNN of [24], our node values are the fixed point of a contraction, but our update function is fixed rather than learned. Our model is closest to InstantGNN [34], which also trains only a classifier on the propagated features, and to APPNP [11], whose propagation also has no learned parameters. Unlike the most popular GNNs, our propagation has no learned weights, no mixing across feature dimensions, and no attention. Maintaining a version with a learned matrix that mixes the features is left open.

2.2 The State

Our goal is to maintain an approximation of the unique fixed point z∗z^{*} in an evolving graph. The idea is to keep an estimate zz of z∗z^{*}, together with a record of how far zz is from being a fixed point. To do this, we maintain three vectors z,y,rz,y,r, which satisfy the following invariants:

Invariant 1.

y=α​s+(1−α)​W​zy=\alpha s+(1-\alpha)Wz.

Invariant 2.

z+r=F⁡(y)z+r=F(y).

Under these invariants, zz is our approximation of z∗z^{*}, and rr is the residual vector containing changes that have not yet been propagated. The vector yy stores the averaged neighbor values after teleportation. It can be recomputed from zz and the current graph, but we maintain it explicitly to support fast graph updates later. If node ii were updated once, its value would change from ziz_{i} to fi​(yi)=zi+rif_{i}(y_{i})=z_{i}+r_{i}. So rir_{i} measures how much node ii would still change, and r=0r=0 exactly when z=z∗z=z^{*}.

The next lemma shows that a small residual implies that zz is close to z∗z^{*}.

Lemma 2.3.

Let (z,y,r)(z,y,r) satisfy Invariants 1 and 2 and, for all ii, |ri|≤(1−K⁡(1−α))​ϵ​d​(i)1−β|r_{i}|\leq(1-K(1-\alpha))\epsilon d(i)^{1-\beta}. Then, for all ii, |zi−zi∗|≤ϵ​d​(i)1−β|z_{i}-z_{i}^{*}|\leq\epsilon d(i)^{1-\beta}.

To prove this lemma, we use the following result, whose proof is given in Appendix A. The proof uses that TT shrinks distances by the factor K⁡(1−α)K(1-\alpha) in the degree-scaled infinity norm, and that z+r=T⁡(z)z+r=T(z) by Invariants 1 and 2.

Lemma 2.4.

Let (z,y,r)(z,y,r) satisfy Invariants 1 and 2. Then, for every ii, |zi−zi∗|≤d​(i)1−β1−K⁡(1−α)​‖Dβ−1​r‖∞|z_{i}-z^{*}_{i}|\leq\frac{d(i)^{1-\beta}}{1-K(1-\alpha)}\|D^{\beta-1}r\|_{\infty}.

The assumption implies ‖Dβ−1​r‖∞≤(1−K⁡(1−α))​ϵ\|D^{\beta-1}r\|_{\infty}\leq(1-K(1-\alpha))\epsilon. The claim now follows from Lemma 2.4. ∎

2.3 Residual Propagation

In this section, we define the push operator. This operator moves the residual rir_{i} into ziz_{i}, which reduces the residual at node ii.

The push operator is shown in Algorithm 1. It takes as input a node ii, the graph GG, and a state (z,y,r)(z,y,r) that is assumed to satisfy Invariants 1 and 2. It returns an updated state (z,y,r)(z,y,r) that also satisfies Invariants 1 and 2. The operator runs in O⁡(d⁡(i))O(d(i)) time.

We prove the following lemma for this procedure.

Lemma 2.5.

Suppose Push(i,G,z,y,r)(i,G,z,y,r) is called on a state (z,y,r)(z,y,r) that satisfies Invariants 1 and 2, and let (z′,y′,r′)(z^{\prime},y^{\prime},r^{\prime}) be the new state. Then (z′,y′,r′)(z^{\prime},y^{\prime},r^{\prime}) also satisfies Invariants 1 and 2. Moreover, for all j≠ij\not=i, |rj′|≤|rj|+K⁡(1−α)​wj​i​|ri|.|r^{\prime}_{j}|\leq|r_{j}|+K(1-\alpha)w_{ji}|r_{i}|. Furthermore, |ri′|≤K⁡(1−α)​wi​i​|ri|.|r^{\prime}_{i}|\leq K(1-\alpha)w_{ii}|r_{i}|.

The proof is given in Appendix A. Combining the push operator with Lemma 2.3 gives a simple algorithm for computing an approximation zz: repeatedly push any node ii whose residual exceeds the bound in Lemma 2.3. When this process terminates, zz is a valid approximation of z∗z^{*}. Algorithm 2 gives the full procedure.

2.4 Graph Updates

In this section, we give an algorithm to maintain a state (z,y,r)(z,y,r) satisfying invariants 1 and 2 after a single edge insertion or deletion.

Suppose an edge (u,v)(u,v) is inserted. Since the degrees of uu and vv change, the invariants are immediately violated for each neighbor of the two endpoints: the degree of each endpoint changes, and so do the normalized edge weights from their neighbors to them. One approach is to iterate over all such neighbors and update their residuals. This is the approach used by [34] in Algorithm 2. However, this takes time at least Ω⁡(d⁡(u)+d⁡(v))\Omega(d(u)+d(v)), which prevents efficient dynamic updates. To avoid this cost, we use a scaling trick introduced by [33]. Define

zu′=(d⁡(u)+1d⁡(u))1−β​zu,zv′=(d⁡(v)+1d⁡(v))1−β​zv,\displaystyle z^{\prime}_{u}=\left(\frac{d(u)+1}{d(u)}\right)^{1-\beta}z_{u},\qquad z^{\prime}_{v}=\left(\frac{d(v)+1}{d(v)}\right)^{1-\beta}z_{v},

and set zw′=zwz^{\prime}_{w}=z_{w} for all other w∉{u,v}w\notin\{u,v\}. Then, for the new state (z′,y′,r′)(z^{\prime},y^{\prime},r^{\prime}), Invariant 1 continues to hold at every node w∉{u,v}w\notin\{u,v\} if we keep yw′=ywy^{\prime}_{w}=y_{w}. Since zw′=zwz^{\prime}_{w}=z_{w} for such nodes, Invariant 2 also continues to hold there if we keep rw′=rwr^{\prime}_{w}=r_{w}. It remains to define yu′,yv′y^{\prime}_{u},y^{\prime}_{v} and ru′,rv′r^{\prime}_{u},r^{\prime}_{v} so that Invariants 1 and 2 hold at the two endpoints. We show that this can be done in O⁡(1)O(1) time, so the full state can be updated in constant time while preserving Invariants 1 and 2. Algorithm 3 gives the details.

We end this section by noting that UpdateEdge preserves Invariants 1 and 2. We formally show this in Lemma A.3 in the Appendix.

2.5 Dynamic Algorithm

Using the procedures defined above, we now give the dynamic algorithm for our non-linear model. We start from an initial state (z0start,y0start,r0start)(z^{\mathrm{start}}_{0},y^{\mathrm{start}}_{0},r^{\mathrm{start}}_{0}) satisfying Invariants 1 and 2, defined by z0start:=0z^{\mathrm{start}}_{0}:=0, y0start:=α​sy^{\mathrm{start}}_{0}:=\alpha s, and r0start:=F⁡(α​s)r^{\mathrm{start}}_{0}:=F(\alpha s). We then apply Cleanup to obtain the post-initial state (z0,y0,r0)(z_{0},y_{0},r_{0}), whose residuals are small enough to give the desired approximation guarantee. After this initialization step, each edge update is handled by first applying UpdateEdge and then applying Cleanup. Algorithm 4 gives the full procedure.

Consider (zt′,yt′,rt′)(z^{\prime}_{t},y^{\prime}_{t},r^{\prime}_{t}) from Algorithm 4, which is the state obtained after applying Eventt\mathrm{Event}_{t} to (zt−1,yt−1,rt−1)(z_{t-1},y_{t-1},r_{t-1}). Let Wt−1,Dt−1W_{t-1},D_{t-1} be the weight and degree matrices before this event, and let Wt,DtW_{t},D_{t} be the corresponding matrices after the event. Then

ΨWt​(rt−1)−ΨWt−1​(rt−1)≤2​ϵ.\Psi_{W_{t}}(r_{t-1})-\Psi_{W_{t-1}}(r_{t-1})\leq 2\epsilon.
Theorem 2.10 (Cost of one edge update).

Let TtT_{t} be the total work of the update at time tt. Then

Tt\displaystyle T_{t} ≤21−K⁡(1−α)+2​(1+2​K​(1−α))​(Bz+ϵ)(1−K⁡(1−α))2​ϵ+ΨWt−1​(rt−1)−ΨWt​(rt)(1−K⁡(1−α))​ϵ.\displaystyle\leq\frac{2}{1-K(1-\alpha)}+\frac{2\left(1+2K(1-\alpha)\right)(B_{z}+\epsilon)}{\left(1-K(1-\alpha)\right)^{2}\epsilon}+\frac{\Psi_{W_{t-1}}(r_{t-1})-\Psi_{W_{t}}(r_{t})}{\left(1-K(1-\alpha)\right)\epsilon}.

We now combine the preceding results to obtain the final upper bound theorem. The proof is given in Appendix A.

Theorem 2.11 (Total cost).

Consider a sequence of kk updates Event1,…,Eventk\mathrm{Event}_{1},\dots,\mathrm{Event}_{k}, and let TtotalT_{\mathrm{total}} denote the total running time of Algorithm 4. Then

Ttotal≤Tinit+2​k1−K⁡(1−α)+2​(1+2​K​(1−α))​(Bz+ϵ)(1−K⁡(1−α))2​ϵ​k,\displaystyle T_{\mathrm{total}}\leq T_{\mathrm{init}}+\frac{2k}{1-K(1-\alpha)}+\frac{2\left(1+2K(1-\alpha)\right)(B_{z}+\epsilon)}{\left(1-K(1-\alpha)\right)^{2}\epsilon}k,

where Tinit=‖D0β​F​(α​s)‖1(1−K⁡(1−α))2​ϵT_{\mathrm{init}}=\frac{\|D_{0}^{\beta}F(\alpha s)\|_{1}}{\left(1-K(1-\alpha)\right)^{2}\epsilon}.

Our analysis of this algorithm is asymptotically tight. The following theorem shows that the amortized time of our algorithm is at least Ω⁡(1/ϵ)\Omega(1/\epsilon), even in the linear case. We provide the proof in Appendix A.

Theorem 2.12 (Lower bound on total cost).

For any sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and any kk, there exists an initial graph with n=Θ⁡(1/ϵ)n=\Theta(1/\epsilon) nodes, a vector ss with ‖s‖∞≤1\|s\|_{\infty}\leq 1, and a sequence of kk edge insertions and deletions such that Algorithm 4 requires a total work of Ω⁡(k/ϵ)\Omega(k/\epsilon). This result holds even in the linear case where fi​(x)=xf_{i}(x)=x for all ii.

3 Exact Dynamic Algorithm For the Linear Case

Our main result concerns approximate maintenance for nonlinear updates, but for completeness, we also provide an exact dynamic result for the linear case. When FF is the identity map, the fixed point is z∗=[I−(1−α)​W]−1​α​sz^{*}=[I-(1-\alpha)W]^{-1}\alpha s. The algorithm adapts the dynamic matrix inverse framework of [23] to the normalized matrix W=D−β​A​Dβ−1W=D^{-\beta}AD^{\beta-1}. Unlike an entry update, one edge update changes the endpoint degrees and hence affects multiple rows and columns of WW. We show how to represent these changes as low-rank updates and how to incorporate them into the lazy update and rebuild scheme of [23]. The details are deferred to Appendix B. We write ω\omega for the exponent of square matrix multiplication. More generally, we write ω⁡(a,b,c)\omega(a,b,c) for the exponent of the running time for multiplying an na×nbn^{a}\times n^{b} matrix by an nb×ncn^{b}\times n^{c} matrix.

Theorem 3.1 (Exact dynamic maintenance for the linear case).

Assume fi​(x)=xf_{i}(x)=x for all ii, and suppose every graph has permanent self-loops. The fixed point z∗z^{*} can be maintained explicitly under (possibly weighted) edge insertions and deletions, with an initialization cost O⁡(nω)O(n^{\omega}) and worst-case update time O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1)−γ+n1+γ)O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)-\gamma}+n^{1+\gamma}\right) for any parameter γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1]. Using current rectangular matrix multiplication bounds, this gives update time O⁡(n1.5275)O(n^{1.5275}).

Proof sketch.

Let B=I−(1−α)​WB=I-(1-\alpha)W. An edge update changes only two rows and two columns of WW, and can be written as a rank-44 update. We then apply the lazy update and periodic rebuild scheme of [23]. Between rebuilds, B−1B^{-1} is maintained implicitly using the Woodbury identity, while the explicit vector z∗=B−1​α​sz^{*}=B^{-1}\alpha s is updated after each edge change. After kk edge updates, one update costs O⁡(n​k+k2)O(nk+k^{2}) time. Following [23], after nγn^{\gamma} updates we rebuild the inverse using the fact that only O⁡(nγ)O(n^{\gamma}) rows and columns have changed. This gives amortized update time O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1)−γ+n1+γ)O(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)-\gamma}+n^{1+\gamma}). The standard deamortization used by [23] gives the same worst-case bound. Full details are in Appendix B. ∎

4 Experiments

We note that our main contribution is the theoretical analysis of the dynamic algorithm (Algorithm 4). Still, we run some experiments to evaluate the practicality of our approach. We organize the experimental contribution into two parts, corresponding to the two main benefits of the model: accuracy and running time. First, in the static setting, we show that adding non-linearity improves predictive accuracy across several benchmark datasets. Second, in the dynamic setting, we evaluate whether our algorithm preserves efficient update performance and compare its running time under non-linearity with the linear algorithm of [34]. We publicly provide our code. 22 2 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/dynamic-nl-public-code-A225

Although the model and analysis are presented for scalar node values, all experiments use multi-dimensional node features. We apply the propagation independently to each feature dimension, using the same graph and parameters for every dimension. All non-linear activations reported in the experiments are uniformly bounded by a constant, and KK-Lipschitz with K≤1K\leq 1.

4.1 Non-linearity Improves Accuracy

We evaluate our approach on several common static datasets. The datasets are explained in Appendix C. Following [34], we first propagate features and then train an MLP on the propagated representations. We use the same activation at every node and pass both the propagated vector zz and the pre-activation vector y=α​s+(1−α)​W​zy=\alpha s+(1-\alpha)Wz to the classifier. Hyperparameters are selected by validation accuracy using the same search space for all activation functions. We use three parameterized activation functions: (i) scaled tanh, tanh⁡(c​x)/c\tanh(cx)/c with parameter cc, denoted by “Sc Tanh cc”; (ii) shifted tanh, tanh⁡(x−c)\tanh(x-c) with parameter cc, denoted by “Sh Tanh cc”; and (iii) hard tanh, min⁡(c,max⁡(−c,x))\min(c,\max(-c,x)) with parameter cc, denoted by “H Tanh cc”.

We compare with GCN [15], GAT [29], Geom-GCN [19], APPNP [11], ACM-GCN [17], and GREAD [7], all of which we run ourselves on the same splits as our model. [20] show that Chameleon and Squirrel contain duplicated nodes and release filtered versions without them, so we also evaluate on these two filtered datasets. Table 1 reports the results on the original datasets, and Table 6 in the Appendix reports the results on the filtered ones. On every dataset, at least one non-linear activation is more accurate than the linear model, and the gain is sometimes large, such as 11 points on Wisconsin. On PubMed and on both filtered datasets, our non-linear model is more accurate than every baseline.

4.2 Dynamic Graphs

We evaluate dynamic propagation on arxiv, products, and SBM-500K [13, 34]. The first two are incremental edge-addition streams from Open Graph Benchmark, while SBM-500K is a synthetic dynamic graph by [34], and contains both insertions and deletions. We compare the linear model with our non-linear hard-tanh model using c=2.5c=2.5. Propagation is parallelized over feature dimensions using 16 CPU cores. For the linear baseline, we use the identity activation function within our framework which yields the same linear propagation model as [34]. We evaluate three update strategies: “scratch”, which recomputes the propagation state after each snapshot; “single”, which applies our dynamic algorithm after each individual edge update; and “batched”, which processes all edge changes within a snapshot prior to cleanup. The “single” strategy aligns with the online update model analyzed in our theorems, whereas “batched” serves as a practical heuristic at the snapshot level.

Figures 1, 2 and 3 show that the linear and non-linear models have similar propagation time and accuracy across all datasets. The dynamic methods are especially beneficial on the larger graphs, where recomputation from scratch is much more expensive. The per-snapshot propagation time is nearly stable after the first snapshot, and cumulative propagation time grows approximately linearly with the number of snapshots, consistent with our amortized update guarantees. All curves in these experiments are averaged over 10 independent runs, and the shaded regions show 95% confidence intervals. Additional experiments in Appendix D show that the observed running times follow the predicted dependence on ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha. We also run larger versions of the SBM benchmark with 2M and 5M nodes, and the papers100M graph from Open Graph Benchmark [13], which has 111M nodes and 1.6B edges (Table 8 in the Appendix). The advantage of dynamic updates over recomputation grows with the size of the graph. On papers100M, a batched update takes about two minutes per snapshot, while recomputation takes over five hours.

5 Conclusion

We studied dynamic maintenance of GNN representations with non-linear propagation. We gave a residual-based push algorithm with an amortized O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\epsilon) update bound under a degree-normalized error guarantee, and we also gave an exact dynamic algorithm for the linear case. Our work has several limitations. First, the propagation is fixed and has no learned weights, so our results do not directly apply to the most popular GNNs. We leave maintaining a model with a learned matrix that mixes the features open. Second, on large dynamic graphs we compare only our linear and non-linear models. Third, we do not theoretically analyze the batched updates used in our experiments. A natural next step is to experiment more with this non-linear propagation model, including more activation functions and learned activation parameters.

After cleanup, the maintained state therefore satisfies |zu|≤ϵ​m|z_{u}|\leq\epsilon m and |zv−1|≤ϵ|z_{v}-1|\leq\epsilon and all residuals are below threshold. In particular, |ru|≤12​ϵ​m|r_{u}|\leq\frac{1}{2}\epsilon m and |rv|≤12​ϵ|r_{v}|\leq\frac{1}{2}\epsilon.

Now insert the edge (u,v)(u,v). We show that the subsequent cleanup must push uu. The update rule scales zuz_{u} by (m+1)/m(m+1)/m and adds the new contribution from vv to uu. Hence the new residual at uu is

ru′=ru+12​zv−zum.\displaystyle r_{u}^{\prime}=r_{u}+\frac{1}{2}z_{v}-\frac{z_{u}}{m}.

Using the bounds above and ϵ​m≤1/100\epsilon m\leq 1/100, we get for ϵ≤1/100\epsilon\leq 1/100,

ru′\displaystyle r_{u}^{\prime} ≥−12​ϵ​m+12​(1−ϵ)−ϵ\displaystyle\geq-\frac{1}{2}\epsilon m+\frac{1}{2}(1-\epsilon)-\epsilon
≥−1200+12​(1−1100)−1100\displaystyle\geq-\frac{1}{200}+\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{1}{100}\right)-\frac{1}{100}
=0.48.\displaystyle=0.48.

On the other hand, the cleanup threshold at uu after the insertion is 12​ϵ​(m+1)≤0.01\frac{1}{2}\epsilon(m+1)\leq 0.01, thus uu has a large residual immediately after the edge update. It remains to check that cleanup cannot remove this residual by pushing other nodes first. Before uu is pushed, the pushes that can affect rur_{u} are pushes at its neighbors.

First consider node vv. After the insertion, d⁡(v)=2d(v)=2, so pushing vv with residual rv′r^{\prime}_{v} changes rur_{u} by (1−α)​wu​v​rv′=rv′/4(1-\alpha)w_{uv}r^{\prime}_{v}=r^{\prime}_{v}/4. The residual left at vv after this push is also rv′/4r^{\prime}_{v}/4. Therefore, even if vv is pushed repeatedly before uu is ever pushed, its total possible effect on rur_{u} has magnitude at most

14​|rv′|+116​|rv′|+164​|rv′|+⋯=13​|rv′|.\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}|r^{\prime}_{v}|+\frac{1}{16}|r^{\prime}_{v}|+\frac{1}{64}|r^{\prime}_{v}|+\cdots=\frac{1}{3}|r^{\prime}_{v}|.

After the insertion, rv′=rv−zv+12⋅zumr^{\prime}_{v}=r_{v}-z_{v}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{z_{u}}{m}. Using bounds before the insertion we have |rv′|≤ϵ/2+(1+ϵ)+ϵ/2=1+2​ϵ|r^{\prime}_{v}|\leq\epsilon/2+(1+\epsilon)+\epsilon/2=1+2\epsilon, so all pushes of vv can reduce rur_{u} by at most (1+2​ϵ)/3≤0.34(1+2\epsilon)/3\leq 0.34.

Now consider the previous leaves. The insertion of (u,v)(u,v) does not change their residuals, because the scaling step preserves the quantity zu/d⁡(u)z_{u}/d(u) that they receive from uu. Thus each leaf ii still has |ri|≤ϵ|r_{i}|\leq\epsilon, since d⁡(i)=2d(i)=2. The same argument as vv shows that all pushes of one leaf can affect rur_{u} by at most |ri|/3|r_{i}|/3. Summing over the m−1m-1 leaves, the total possible effect from all leaves is at most 13​(m−1)​ϵ≤1300\frac{1}{3}(m-1)\epsilon\leq\frac{1}{300}.

Therefore, before the first push of uu, even after all possible pushes of vv and all leaves, the residual at uu is still at least 0.48−0.34−1300>0.10.48-0.34-\frac{1}{300}>0.1. This is larger than the cleanup threshold at uu, which is below 0.010.01. Hence, cleanup cannot terminate before pushing uu.

Pushing uu costs Θ⁡(d⁡(u))=Θ⁡(m)=Θ⁡(1/ϵ)\Theta(d(u))=\Theta(m)=\Theta(1/\epsilon) work. Thus every insertion of (u,v)(u,v) forces Ω⁡(1/ϵ)\Omega(1/\epsilon) work.

Finally, take the update sequence that repeatedly toggles the edge (u,v)(u,v). After every deletion and cleanup, the graph is again the initial graph, so the same argument applies to the next insertion. Therefore, the total work is Ω⁡(k/ϵ)\Omega(k/\epsilon), and the amortized update time is Ω⁡(1/ϵ)\Omega(1/\epsilon). ∎

Appendix B Exact Dynamic Algorithm For the Linear Case

In this section, we focus on the linear case, which is closely related to the PageRank problem. We seek an algorithm that computes the exact solution instead of an approximation. As before, we assume that the graph contains permanent self-loops. However, we do not require the graph to be unweighted, and we define the degree of a node as the sum of the weights of its incident edges. Suppose that each fif_{i} is the identity function. Then the unique fixed point of the system is

z∗=[I−(1−α)​W]−1​α​s.z^{*}=\left[I-(1-\alpha)W\right]^{-1}\alpha s. (5)

For a static graph, one can compute z∗z^{*} exactly by computing the matrix inverse [I−(1−α)​W]−1\left[I-(1-\alpha)W\right]^{-1} in O⁡(nω)O(n^{\omega}) time, where ω\omega is the matrix multiplication exponent [6]. For a dynamic graph, there is an extensive line of work on dynamic matrix inverse and dynamic systems of linear equations. We adapt these results to the PageRank model, and in particular to the normalized weight matrix. Our algorithms are mainly inspired by the dynamic algorithm for systems of linear equations of [23]. However, their algorithm does not directly give a dynamic algorithm for computing z∗z^{*} in our setting, because an edge insertion or deletion may change up to two rows and two columns of WW due to the normalized weights. Their algorithm does not directly support such updates. One could try to decompose the changes caused by an insertion or deletion into multiple operations, but this requires care, since their algorithm assumes that the matrix remains non-singular after each intermediate update.

In the following lemma, we show that an edge update induces a low-rank update to WW. This directly follows from the fact that only two rows and two columns can change. However, the specific structure of the update is what allows us to obtain an efficient algorithm.

Lemma B.1.

Suppose an edge between u,vu,v with weight δ\delta is inserted or deleted from the graph, and let W+W_{+} be the normalized weight matrix of the new graph. Then

W+=W+U​VT\displaystyle W_{+}=W+UV^{T}

for some U,V∈ℝn×4U,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 4}. In other words, the edge update induces an update of rank at most 4 to WW.

Proof.

We use the subscript ++ to denote quantities after the update. Let the signed change be η=δ\eta=\delta for an insertion and η=−δ\eta=-\delta for a deletion. Let E=[euev].E=\begin{bmatrix}e_{u}&e_{v}\end{bmatrix}. Then A+=A+η⁡(eu​evT+ev​euT)A_{+}=A+\eta(e_{u}e_{v}^{T}+e_{v}e_{u}^{T}) and D+=D+η⁡(eu​euT+ev​evT).D_{+}=D+\eta(e_{u}e_{u}^{T}+e_{v}e_{v}^{T}). Let W=D−β​A​Dβ−1W=D^{-\beta}AD^{\beta-1} and W+=D+−β​A+​D+β−1W_{+}=D_{+}^{-\beta}A_{+}D_{+}^{\beta-1}.

Since only the degrees of uu and vv change, there are diagonal matrices Λ,Γ∈ℝ2×2\Lambda,\Gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} such that D+−β​Dβ=I+E​Λ​ETD_{+}^{-\beta}D^{\beta}=I+E\Lambda E^{T} and D1−β​D+β−1=I+E​Γ​ET.D^{1-\beta}D_{+}^{\beta-1}=I+E\Gamma E^{T}. For i∈{u,v}i\in\{u,v\}, these matrices have entries Λi​i=(di/di,+)β−1\Lambda_{ii}=(d_{i}/d_{i,+})^{\beta}-1 and Γi​i=(di,+/di)β−1−1.\Gamma_{ii}=(d_{i,+}/d_{i})^{\beta-1}-1.

Define H∈ℝ2×2H\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} by E​H​ET=η​D+−β​(eu​evT+ev​euT)​D+β−1.EHE^{T}=\eta D_{+}^{-\beta}(e_{u}e_{v}^{T}+e_{v}e_{u}^{T})D_{+}^{\beta-1}. Equivalently, Hu​v=η​du,+−β​dv,+β−1,H_{uv}=\eta d_{u,+}^{-\beta}d_{v,+}^{\beta-1}, Hv​u=η​dv,+−β​du,+β−1,H_{vu}=\eta d_{v,+}^{-\beta}d_{u,+}^{\beta-1}, and the diagonal entries of HH are zero.

Using these definitions,

W+=D+−β​A+​D+β−1=(I+E​Λ​ET)​W​(I+E​Γ​ET)+E​H​ET.W_{+}=D_{+}^{-\beta}A_{+}D_{+}^{\beta-1}=(I+E\Lambda E^{T})W(I+E\Gamma E^{T})+EHE^{T}.

Thus

W+−W=E​Λ​ET​W​(I+E​Γ​ET)+W​E​Γ​ET+E​H​ET.W_{+}-W=E\Lambda E^{T}W(I+E\Gamma E^{T})+WE\Gamma E^{T}+EHE^{T}.

Now set

U=[EW​E​Γ]∈ℝn×4U=\begin{bmatrix}E&WE\Gamma\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 4}

and

VT=[Λ​ET​W​(I+E​Γ​ET)+H​ETET]∈ℝ4×n.V^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}\Lambda E^{T}W(I+E\Gamma E^{T})+HE^{T}\\ E^{T}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times n}.

Then W+=W+U​VTW_{+}=W+UV^{T}, so the update has rank at most 44. ∎

Next, we describe at a high level how z∗z^{*} can be maintained under updates. To do this, we use the Woodbury matrix identity [30], which gives a formula for the inverse of a matrix under a low-rank update.

Let B:=I−(1−α)​WB:=I-(1-\alpha)W. Following [23], we maintain B−1B^{-1} in an implicit form. Specifically, after kk updates, we write B=B0+𝒰​𝒱TB=B_{0}+\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}^{T}, where 𝒰,𝒱∈ℝn×4​k\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 4k} and B0B_{0} is the last rebuilt matrix. We maintain M:=B0−1M:=B_{0}^{-1}, Y:=M​𝒰Y:=M\mathcal{U}, and the small inverse G:=(I4​k+𝒱T​Y)−1G:=(I_{4k}+\mathcal{V}^{T}Y)^{-1}. We also maintain the current solution z∗=B−1​α​sz^{*}=B^{-1}\alpha s. By the Woodbury identity,

B−1=M−Y​G​𝒱T​M.B^{-1}=M-YG\mathcal{V}^{T}M. (6)

We use the subscript ++ to denote the state after a single edge update. Consider an update from WW to W+W_{+}. By Lemma B.1, W+=W+UW​VWTW_{+}=W+U_{W}V_{W}^{T} for some UW,VW∈ℝn×4U_{W},V_{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 4}. Then B+=B+U​VTB_{+}=B+UV^{T}, where U=UWU=U_{W} and V=−(1−α)​VWV=-(1-\alpha)V_{W}. Define Z:=B−1​UZ:=B^{-1}U and S:=I4+VT​ZS:=I_{4}+V^{T}Z. Applying the Woodbury identity again gives B+−1=B−1−Z​S−1​VT​B−1B_{+}^{-1}=B^{-1}-ZS^{-1}V^{T}B^{-1}. Since SS has size 4×44\times 4, its inverse can be computed in O⁡(1)O(1) time. The new solution is therefore z+∗=z∗−Z​S−1​VT​z∗z^{*}_{+}=z^{*}-ZS^{-1}V^{T}z^{*}. Once ZZ is known, this update takes O⁡(n)O(n) time. We give the details for computing ZZ in the lemma below.

Lemma B.2.

Let an edge update produce B+=B+U​VTB_{+}=B+UV^{T} with U,V∈ℝn×4U,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 4}. Then the maintained state and the solution z+∗=B+−1​α​sz^{*}_{+}=B_{+}^{-1}\alpha s can be updated in time O⁡(n​k+k2)O(nk+k^{2}).

Proof.

Before the update, we maintain B=B0+𝒰​𝒱T,B=B_{0}+\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}^{T}, where 𝒰,𝒱∈ℝn×4​k\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 4k}, M=B0−1,M=B_{0}^{-1}, Y=M​𝒰,Y=M\mathcal{U}, G=(I+𝒱T​Y)−1,G=(I+\mathcal{V}^{T}Y)^{-1}, and z∗=B−1​α​s.z^{*}=B^{-1}\alpha s. Thus

B−1=M−Y​G​𝒱T​M.B^{-1}=M-YG\mathcal{V}^{T}M.

By Lemma B.1, the edge update has U=[EW​E​Γ],U=\begin{bmatrix}E&WE\Gamma\end{bmatrix}, where E=[euev]E=\begin{bmatrix}e_{u}&e_{v}\end{bmatrix} and Γ∈ℝ2×2\Gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} is diagonal. We first compute Z=B−1​UZ=B^{-1}U. Since B=I−(1−α)​WB=I-(1-\alpha)W, B−1​W=11−α​(B−1−I).B^{-1}W=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}(B^{-1}-I). Therefore,

Z=[B−1​E11−α​(B−1​E−E)​Γ].Z=\begin{bmatrix}B^{-1}E&\frac{1}{1-\alpha}(B^{-1}E-E)\Gamma\end{bmatrix}.

It remains to compute B−1​EB^{-1}E. Using the maintained inverse representation,

B−1​E=M​E−Y​G​𝒱T​M​E.B^{-1}E=ME-YG\mathcal{V}^{T}ME.

The matrix M​EME consists of two columns of MM, so it can be obtained in O⁡(n)O(n) time. Computing 𝒱T​M​E\mathcal{V}^{T}ME costs O⁡(n​k)O(nk), multiplying by GG costs O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}), and multiplying by YY costs O⁡(n​k)O(nk). Hence ZZ can be computed in O⁡(n​k+k2)O(nk+k^{2}) time.

Now define S=I4+VT​Z.S=I_{4}+V^{T}Z. Since SS is 4×44\times 4, computing S−1S^{-1} takes O⁡(1)O(1) time. By the Woodbury identity,

B+−1=B−1−Z​S−1​VT​B−1.B_{+}^{-1}=B^{-1}-ZS^{-1}V^{T}B^{-1}.

Therefore, z+∗=z∗−Z​S−1​VT​z∗.z^{*}_{+}=z^{*}-ZS^{-1}V^{T}z^{*}. The product VT​z∗V^{T}z^{*} costs O⁡(n)O(n) time, and the remaining operations also cost O⁡(n)O(n) time. This is within the claimed bound.

It remains to update the maintained state. We append the new factors: 𝒰+=[𝒰U]\mathcal{U}_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{U}&U\end{bmatrix} and 𝒱+=[𝒱V].\mathcal{V}_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{V}&V\end{bmatrix}. We also append M​UMU to YY. The first two columns, M​EME, are already available. For the remaining two columns, M​W​E​ΓMWE\Gamma, use B0=I−(1−α)​W0B_{0}=I-(1-\alpha)W_{0} and B=B0+𝒰​𝒱T=I−(1−α)​W.B=B_{0}+\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}^{T}=I-(1-\alpha)W. These identities imply W=W0−11−α​𝒰​𝒱T.W=W_{0}-\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}^{T}. Thus

M​W​E=11−α​(M​E−E)−11−α​Y​𝒱T​E.MWE=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}(ME-E)-\frac{1}{1-\alpha}Y\mathcal{V}^{T}E.

Therefore,

M​U=[M​E(11−α​(M​E−E)−11−α​Y​𝒱T​E)​Γ].MU=\begin{bmatrix}ME&\left(\frac{1}{1-\alpha}(ME-E)-\frac{1}{1-\alpha}Y\mathcal{V}^{T}E\right)\Gamma\end{bmatrix}.

This costs O⁡(n​k)O(nk) time to compute, so Y+=[YM​U]Y_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}Y&MU\end{bmatrix} can be updated in O⁡(n​k)O(nk) time.

Finally, we update G+=(I4​(k+1)+𝒱+T​Y+)−1.G_{+}=(I_{4(k+1)}+\mathcal{V}_{+}^{T}Y_{+})^{-1}. After appending the new factors, we have 𝒰+=[𝒰U],𝒱+=[𝒱V],Y+=M​𝒰+=[YM​U].\mathcal{U}_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{U}&U\end{bmatrix},\mathcal{V}_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathcal{V}&V\end{bmatrix},Y_{+}=M\mathcal{U}_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}Y&MU\end{bmatrix}. Therefore,

I4​(k+1)+𝒱+T​Y+\displaystyle I_{4(k+1)}+\mathcal{V}_{+}^{T}Y_{+} =[I4​k+𝒱T​Y𝒱T​M​UVT​YI4+VT​M​U].\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}I_{4k}+\mathcal{V}^{T}Y&\mathcal{V}^{T}MU\\ V^{T}Y&I_{4}+V^{T}MU\end{bmatrix}.

Since G=(I4​k+𝒱T​Y)−1G=(I_{4k}+\mathcal{V}^{T}Y)^{-1} is already stored, we only need to invert this block matrix. Define

C:=𝒱T​M​U∈ℝ4​k×4,R:=VT​Y∈ℝ4×4​k,Q:=I4+VT​M​U∈ℝ4×4.C:=\mathcal{V}^{T}MU\in\mathbb{R}^{4k\times 4},\qquad R:=V^{T}Y\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4k},\qquad Q:=I_{4}+V^{T}MU\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4}.

Then

I4​(k+1)+𝒱+T​Y+=[G−1CRQ].I_{4(k+1)}+\mathcal{V}_{+}^{T}Y_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}G^{-1}&C\\ R&Q\end{bmatrix}.

Let Σ:=Q−R​G​C∈ℝ4×4\Sigma:=Q-RGC\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 4} be the Schur complement. By the block inverse formula,

G+=[G+G​C​Σ−1​R​G−G​C​Σ−1−Σ−1​R​GΣ−1].G_{+}=\begin{bmatrix}G+GC\Sigma^{-1}RG&-GC\Sigma^{-1}\\ -\Sigma^{-1}RG&\Sigma^{-1}\end{bmatrix}.

It remains to bound the cost of forming this expression. The matrix M​UMU has already been computed. Forming C=𝒱T​M​UC=\mathcal{V}^{T}MU costs O⁡(n​k)O(nk) time, forming R=VT​YR=V^{T}Y costs O⁡(n​k)O(nk) time, and forming Q=I4+VT​M​UQ=I_{4}+V^{T}MU costs O⁡(n)O(n) time. Computing G​CGC and R​GRG costs O⁡(k2)O(k^{2}) time, since GG has size 4​k×4​k4k\times 4k. The matrix Σ\Sigma has size 4×44\times 4, so computing Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} costs O⁡(1)O(1) time. Hence updating G+G_{+} costs O⁡(n​k+k2)O(nk+k^{2}) time.

Thus both the maintained state and the solution z+∗=B+−1​α​sz^{*}_{+}=B_{+}^{-1}\alpha s can be updated in O⁡(n​k+k2)O(nk+k^{2}) time. ∎

The above lemma gives an efficient algorithm as long as kk is small. Thus, as kk grows, we need a way to propagate all changes into BB and make 𝒰,𝒱\mathcal{U},\mathcal{V} small again. The following lemma gives this rebuilding step. We use the rebuilding algorithm of [23, Theorem 2], but state it here explicitly to avoid ambiguity. The theorem and proof of [23] are stated for the case where O⁡(nγ)O(n^{\gamma}) columns of the original matrix have changed. We note that the proof extends directly to the case where O⁡(nγ)O(n^{\gamma}) columns and O⁡(nγ)O(n^{\gamma}) rows have changed. We state this form in the following lemma.

Lemma B.3.

Let AA be nonsingular, and suppose A′=A+ΔA^{\prime}=A+\Delta is also nonsingular. Assume that Δ\Delta is supported only on rows and columns indexed by a set SS, where |S|=k=O⁡(nγ)|S|=k=O(n^{\gamma}). Then A−1A^{-1} can be updated to (A′)−1(A^{\prime})^{-1} using O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1))O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)}\right) arithmetic operations.

Proof.

Let E∈ℝn×kE\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k} be the matrix whose columns are the standard basis vectors indexed by SS. Since Δ\Delta is supported on S×[n]∪[n]×S,S\times[n]\cup[n]\times S, we can write Δ=E​R+C​ET,\Delta=ER+CE^{T}, where R=ET​ΔR=E^{T}\Delta contains the changed rows, and C=(I−E​ET)​Δ​EC=(I-EE^{T})\Delta E contains the changed columns outside those rows.

Thus A′=A+E​R+C​ET=A+U​VT,A^{\prime}=A+ER+CE^{T}=A+UV^{T}, where

U=[EC],VT=[RET].U=\begin{bmatrix}E&C\end{bmatrix},\qquad V^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}R\\ E^{T}\end{bmatrix}.

Hence U,V∈ℝn×2​kU,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 2k}, so the update has rank at most 2​k2k. By the Woodbury identity,

(A′)−1=A−1−A−1​U​(I2​k+VT​A−1​U)−1​VT​A−1.(A^{\prime})^{-1}=A^{-1}-A^{-1}U\left(I_{2k}+V^{T}A^{-1}U\right)^{-1}V^{T}A^{-1}.

The products A−1​UA^{-1}U and VT​A−1V^{T}A^{-1} are rectangular products with one dimension O⁡(k)=O⁡(nγ)O(k)=O(n^{\gamma}), so they cost O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1))O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)}\right) arithmetic operations. The middle matrix has size O⁡(k)×O⁡(k)O(k)\times O(k), and the final product has dimensions n×O⁡(k)n\times O(k) by O⁡(k)×n.O(k)\times n. These steps are within the same bound. Therefore the full update costs O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1))O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)}\right) arithmetic operations. ∎

Using the above lemma, we rebuild after nγn^{\gamma} updates.

Corollary B.4.

After nγn^{\gamma} edge updates, the inverse B−1B^{-1} can be rebuilt in O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1))O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)}\right) arithmetic operations.

Proof.

Each edge update changes at most two rows and two columns. Therefore, after nγn^{\gamma} edge updates, the total change is supported on O⁡(nγ)O(n^{\gamma}) rows and O⁡(nγ)O(n^{\gamma}) columns. By Lemma B.3, we can compute the updated inverse B−1B^{-1} in O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1))O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)}\right) arithmetic operations. ∎

Combining the above results gives the following theorem.

Theorem B.5.

The fixed point z∗z^{*} can be maintained by an algorithm with O⁡(nω)O(n^{\omega}) initialization cost and O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1)−γ+n1+γ)O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)-\gamma}+n^{1+\gamma}\right) worst-case update time. The algorithm maintains z∗z^{*} explicitly after each update. In particular, setting γ≈0.5275\gamma\approx 0.5275 gives update time O⁡(n1.5275)O\left(n^{1.5275}\right) under the current known bounds.

Proof.

We begin by computing M=B−1M=B^{-1} in O⁡(nω)O(n^{\omega}) time. We then process updates using the lazy representation and rebuild after O⁡(nγ)O(n^{\gamma}) updates. By Lemma B.2, each lazy update costs O⁡(n1+γ)O\left(n^{1+\gamma}\right) time. By Corollary B.4, each rebuild costs O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1))O(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)}) time. This gives the stated bound in amortized time.

To obtain the same bound in worst-case time, we use the standard deamortization technique noted by [23]. We maintain two copies of the data structure. The active copy answers queries and processes updates using the lazy Woodbury representation. In parallel, the second copy performs the rebuild incrementally over the next nγn^{\gamma} updates. By spreading the O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1))O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)}\right) rebuild work evenly over these updates, the rebuild contributes O⁡(nω⁡(1,γ,1)−γ)O\left(n^{\omega(1,\gamma,1)-\gamma}\right) worst-case time per update. At the end of the phase, the rebuilt copy becomes active. Using the matrix multiplication bounds of [1] and the interpolation method for ω⁡(1,γ,1)\omega(1,\gamma,1) from [28], we optimize over γ\gamma and obtain γ≈0.5275\gamma\approx 0.5275, which gives the claimed bound. ∎

Appendix C Experiment Details of Section 4.1

This section describes the experimental setup for Table 1. We provide the general setup, the hyperparameter search and the configurations selected for each cell of Table 1 in Section C.1, and a discussion of the Chameleon and Squirrel datasets in Section C.2.

Datasets.

We consider several common datasets. All datasets contain feature vectors for all nodes, and labels for a subset of nodes are provided in the training set. Cora, Citeseer [25], and PubMed [18] are citation graphs, where nodes are papers and edges are citations. Actor [26, 19] is a graph of actors, where edges denote co-occurrence on the same Wikipedia page. WebKB [8] is a dataset collected from university websites where nodes represent webpages, and edges represent links between them. We use the Cornell, Wisconsin, and Texas graphs from this dataset. Chameleon and Squirrel are graphs of Wikipedia pages on specific topics [22, 19], where nodes are pages and edges are mutual links between them. For a discussion of Chameleon and Squirrel, see Section C.2.

Splits.

All datasets are loaded through PyTorch Geometric [10]. Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed use the standard Planetoid train/validation/test split [32]. Cornell, Texas, Wisconsin (WebKB), Actor, Chameleon, and Squirrel use the ten random 48%/32%/20%48\%/32\%/20\% splits released by [19]. We make every graph undirected and standardize each feature column to have zero mean and unit variance. Table 3 shows the scales of the datasets used in these experiments.

The PyTorch Geometric Planetoid distributions of Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed are MIT licensed, with the underlying Pubmed records also subject to the NLM Data License. The WebKB graphs and Actor are loaded through PyTorch Geometric, but their standalone dataset licenses appear unspecified. Chameleon and Squirrel, including the filtered versions released by [20], are distributed under the MIT license.

Method.

Following [34], we first propagate the features using the PageRank model and then train an MLP on the propagated features using the training labels. For the non-linear model, we use the same activation function for all node functions fif_{i}. In addition to the propagated features zz, we pass the pre-activation vectors y=α​s+(1−α)​W​zy=\alpha s+(1-\alpha)Wz to the MLP. When the activation function is the identity, y≈zy\approx z.

Baselines.

We ran every baseline in Table 1 ourselves, on exactly the same splits as our model: GCN [15], GAT [29], Geom-GCN [19], APPNP [11], ACM-GCN [17], and GREAD [7]. When the authors of a method published a configuration for a dataset and split, we used it. Otherwise, we tuned the method over at most 288 configurations, the same size our model uses for each activation function. The tuning has two stages. We first rank the configurations by validation accuracy on one seed. We then rerun the best configurations on five new seeds, select the one with the highest validation accuracy, and report its test accuracy from these runs. We report standard errors in the same way as for our model.

Propagation.

After normalization, we multiply the features by a feature scale cfeatc_{\mathrm{feat}} before propagation. The classifier receives the concatenation [y,z][y,z], where y=α​s+(1−α)​W​zy=\alpha s+(1-\alpha)Wz is the pre-activation vector. We include cfeatc_{\mathrm{feat}} in the search grid because it interacts with the saturation thresholds of activations such as tanh.

Activations.

We evaluate the linear baseline (denoted “Linear”), tanh\tanh, sigmoid\mathrm{sigmoid}, scaled tanh with c∈{0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,5,6,8}c\in\{0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,5,6,8\}, hard tanh with c∈{0.3,0.5,0.7,1,1.5,2,2.5}c\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7,1,1.5,2,2.5\}, and shifted tanh with c∈{0.5,−0.5,−0.9,−1.2}c\in\{0.5,-0.5,-0.9,-1.2\}. This broad set lets us test activations with different shapes and saturation behavior. Table 1 reports only the activations that achieve the best test accuracy in at least one dataset column; the remaining activations were also evaluated.

Classifier.

The classifier is either a linear layer or a one-hidden-layer MLP with hidden width 512512, ReLU, and dropout 0.50.5. The classifier type is selected as part of the search grid. Both classifiers are trained with Adam on the cross-entropy loss, with weight decay 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, for at most 400400 epochs. We use early stopping after 100100 epochs without improvement in validation accuracy. We report the test accuracy at the epoch with the highest validation accuracy.

Compute.

Each run for an (activation, dataset, seed, split, hyperparameter) configuration uses one NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU, 4GB RAM, and 2 CPU cores and takes less than 5 seconds to complete.

C.1 Hyperparameter Sweep and Selected Configurations

We use the same search grid in Table 4 for every (activation, dataset) pair. For each (activation, dataset) cell, we evaluate every grid point on 55 random seeds for each of the 1010 splits described above, for a total of 5050 runs per configuration. We then select the grid point with the highest mean validation accuracy across these runs. In Table 1, we report the mean and standard error of the test accuracy for the selected grid point. The selected configurations are listed in Table 5.

C.2 Chameleon and Squirrel

Chameleon and Squirrel [22] are Wikipedia link networks that are widely used as heterophilous benchmarks. [20] show that the publicly distributed versions of these datasets contain duplicated nodes, which can leak across the train, validation, and test splits. This leakage can increase the accuracy of methods that effectively memorize duplicated nodes. They release filtered versions with the duplicated nodes removed. The results in Table 1 use the original Geom-GCN preprocessed splits, which are standard for these datasets. Table 6 reports our model and the baselines on the filtered versions, using the ten splits of [20]. For our model, we use the same hyperparameter search grid as in Section C.1, and Table 7 shows the selected hyperparameters. The baselines are tuned as described in Appendix C. We do not include Geom-GCN, because its authors released the data it needs only for the original graphs.

Appendix D Experiment Details of Section 4.2

Datasets and snapshots.

We use two graphs from the Open Graph Benchmark [13]: arxiv, a citation network, and products, the Amazon products co-purchasing network. We also use the synthetic SBM-500K dataset generated by [34]. The edge updates for arxiv and products are incremental edge additions, while SBM-500K includes both edge additions and edge deletions. The arxiv and products benchmarks are used with their official train/validation/test splits. We follow the snapshot split protocol of [34]. First, we make the graph undirected and standardize every feature column to have zero mean and unit variance. We then remove every non-self edge incident to a training node. The remaining edges form the initial graph, and the removed edges form the insertion stream. The insertion stream is shuffled with constant random seed and split into contiguous snapshots. We use 1616 snapshots for arxiv, 1515 snapshots for products, and SBM-500K contains 10 snapshots. Self-loops are present throughout the experiment and are not part of the update stream.

For SBM-500K, the dataset is generated with the InstantGNN [34] SBM generator3 using 500,000500{,}000 nodes, 5050 communities, average in-community degree 2020, average out-community degree 11, 1010 snapshots, and 2,5002{,}500 changed nodes per snapshot. The dataset provides initial labels and per-snapshot labels. Since features and splits are not shipped with the text edge stream, we generate fixed-seed sparse random features with 256256 dimensions and 1616 nonzero entries per node, standardize every feature column, and use random train/validation/test splits of 70%/20%/10%70\%/20\%/10\%.

Under this construction, arxiv has 169,343169{,}343 nodes, 128128 features, 213,848213{,}848 initial undirected non-self edges, and 1,157,7991{,}157{,}799 total undirected non-self edges after all insertions. The products graph has 2,449,0292{,}449{,}029 nodes, 100100 features, 33,592,70833{,}592{,}708 initial undirected non-self edges, and 61,859,01261{,}859{,}012 total undirected non-self edges after all insertions. The SBM-500K graph has 500,000500{,}000 nodes, 256256 generated features, 5050 classes, 6,820,8316{,}820{,}831 initial undirected non-self edges, and 6,823,9826{,}823{,}982 final undirected non-self edges after all updates. Across its 1010 snapshots, the stream contains 1,263,7391{,}263{,}739 unique undirected edge-update events, consisting of 633,445633{,}445 insertions and 630,294630{,}294 deletions.

Dataset licenses.

The Open Graph Benchmark lists arxiv under ODC-BY and products under the Amazon License. The SBM datasets are synthetic datasets generated using the code 33 3 https://github.com/zheng-yp/InstantGNN from InstantGNN [34]; the repository does not specify a license for these datasets.

Propagation methods.

For both the linear and non-linear models, we use β=0.5,ϵ=10−7.\beta=0.5,\ \epsilon=10^{-7}. We use α=0.1\alpha=0.1 for arxiv and products, and α=0.001\alpha=0.001 for SBM-500K.

Before propagation, we multiply the standardized input features by 33. The linear model uses the identity activation. The non-linear model uses hard tanh, f⁡(x)=min⁡(2.5,max⁡(−2.5,x)).f(x)=\min(2.5,\max(-2.5,x)). We use the same activation for every node and every feature dimension.

We compare three propagation strategies. The “scratch” method applies all edge updates in the current snapshot, resets the propagation state to the canonical initialization, and runs cleanup from scratch. The “batched” method applies all insertions in the current snapshot as one batch and then runs cleanup once. The “single” method applies insertions one edge at a time, runs the dynamic update after each edge, and returns the maintained representation after every edge insertion; for reporting, we evaluate the representation after the last edge of each snapshot. Thus, “single” solves the strictly stronger online problem, while “batched” matches the snapshot update used in [34].

Propagation is implemented in C++. The implementation stores the feature, propagated, pre-activation, and residual arrays as dense double-precision arrays of shape F×nF\times n. Cleanup is run independently for each feature dimension, and dimensions are parallelized with OpenMP. We use the same approximation guarantees as [34].

Classifier and parameters.

After each initial propagation or snapshot update, we train a classifier from scratch on the current propagated features. The classifier input is the concatenation [z,y][z,y], where y=α​s+(1−α)​W​zy=\alpha s+(1-\alpha)Wz is the pre-activation vector. For arxiv and products, the classifier is a 44-layer MLP with hidden width 10241024, batch normalization after hidden linear layers, ReLU activations, and Adam optimization with learning rate 10−410^{-4} and no weight decay. For SBM-500K, we use a 22-layer MLP with hidden width 10241024, dropout 0.10.1, Adam learning rate 0.010.01, and no weight decay. We train arxiv and products for at most 10001000 epochs and SBM-500K for at most 200200 epochs, with early stopping after 5050 epochs without validation improvement. We use dropout 0.30.3 on arxiv, dropout 0.50.5 on products, and dropout 0.10.1 on SBM-500K. The arxiv classifier is trained full-batch, while products uses mini-batches of size 512512 and SBM-500K uses mini-batches of size 10241024.

These parameters were all inherited from experiments of [34].

Compute.

Each dynamic experiment on arxiv, products, and SBM-500K is run with one NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU, 1616 CPU cores, and 3232GB RAM. The runs for Table 8 use 1616 CPU cores and no GPU. They need about 99GB of RAM on SBM-500K, 3232GB on SBM-2M, 7777GB on SBM-5M, and 700700GB on papers100M.

Reported quantities.

The accuracy plots report the test accuracy of the classifier trained on the propagated features available at each snapshot. The cumulative-time plots report the cumulative propagation time, including the initial propagation and all processed snapshots. The per-snapshot time plots report only propagation time for the corresponding initial graph or snapshot update; classifier training time is excluded from these timing plots.

Larger graphs.

We also run two larger versions of the SBM benchmark, SBM-2M and SBM-5M, and the papers100M graph from Open Graph Benchmark [13], which has 111M nodes and 1.6B edges. Table 8 reports the propagation time per snapshot. The cost of recomputation grows with the size of the graph, while the cost of dynamic updates does not. We generate SBM-2M and SBM-5M with the same InstantGNN generator as SBM-500K, changing only the number of nodes. We scale the number of communities so that each community has 10,00010{,}000 nodes, and keep the degrees, the 1010 snapshots, and the 2,5002{,}500 changed nodes per snapshot. So each snapshot has about 126,000126{,}000 edge updates at every size. We use the same α\alpha, β\beta, and ϵ\epsilon as for SBM-500K. For papers100M, we follow the same snapshot split protocol as for arxiv and products, with 2020 snapshots of about 22M edge insertions each. We use α=0.1\alpha=0.1, β=0.5\beta=0.5, and ϵ=2.2×10−9\epsilon=2.2\times 10^{-9}. We run each SBM setting with 55 random seeds and papers100M once.

Varying ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha.

To study how the parameters affect running time, we repeat the same experiment while varying ϵ\epsilon and α\alpha on the arxiv and SBM-500K datasets. Figures 4 and 5 show the results. We find that the observed running times are consistent with the theoretical dependence on these parameters. For Figures 4 and 5, we vary ϵ∈{10−7,10−6,10−5,10−4,10−3}\epsilon\in\{10^{-7},10^{-6},10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3}\} and α∈{0.001,0.01,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7}\alpha\in\{0.001,0.01,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.5,0.7\}, respectively. We run each setting with two random seeds and report the mean over the two runs.
